levels.title: Measurement and Applied Planning: Numbers You Can Defend

units.title: Measuring Cost, Cash and Return Before Comparing Anything

lessons.title: Amortization: how one fixed payment splits into interest and principal
lessons.explanation: An amortizing loan makes the same payment every period and reaches a zero balance exactly at the end of the term. The payment is fixed; the split inside it is not. Each period the lender charges interest on the balance still outstanding, and whatever remains of the payment after that charge reduces the balance. Because the balance starts high, the first payments are mostly interest. Because the balance falls, later payments carry less interest, so the principal portion grows even though nobody changes the payment. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes the sequence directly: at the beginning of a mortgage term you owe more interest because the balance is still high and most of the payment goes to interest; as the principal is paid down you owe less interest each month, so more of the payment goes to principal; and near the end most of the payment goes to the last of the principal. The Bureau adds that lenders use a standard formula to set the payment so the loan is paid off precisely at the end of the term. Two consequences run through the rest of this level. First, the cost of borrowing is not the rate multiplied by the amount: interest is charged on a shrinking balance, so total interest is far smaller than rate times principal times time. Second, interest is concentrated in the early periods, so any decision to prepay, refinance or stretch a term has to be read against a schedule rather than against the size of the payment.
lessons.example: Take an assumed $32,000 loan at 6 percent a year repaid over 36 monthly payments. Because payments are monthly, the periodic rate is 6 percent divided by 12, which is 0.5 percent, and the number of periods is 36. That is exactly the adjustment OpenStax makes in its loan amortization section when it converts an annual rate to a monthly rate and years into months. The fixed payment is $973.50. In month 1 the interest charge is 0.5 percent of $32,000, which is $160.00, so principal in that payment is $973.50 minus $160.00, or $813.50. By month 18 the balance has fallen far enough that interest is $88.02 and principal is $885.49. By month 36 interest is $4.84 and principal is $968.66. The interest share of the payment falls from 16.4 percent to 0.5 percent while the payment itself never moves. Total interest over the three years is $3,046.07 and total payments are $35,046.07. Change one term and the picture changes. Stretch the same $32,000 over 60 months and the payment falls to $618.65 while total interest rises to $5,118.98, which is $2,072.91 more. Keep 36 months and add $100 a month instead: the loan clears in 33 months and interest falls to $2,738.94, a saving of $307.13. One further number is worth carrying: of the $3,046.07 of interest, $2,240.76, or 73.6 percent, is paid inside the first 18 months. Assumptions for every figure: fixed rate, no fees, no insurance, no escrow, monthly compounding at one twelfth of the annual rate, payments at the end of each month, no late or missed payments, and no added borrowing. Change any of those and the schedule must be recomputed.
lessons.question: What is the interest charge in the first month of a $32,000 loan at an assumed 6 percent annual rate with monthly payments, and why is the later interest charge on the same loan smaller?
lessons.answer: The first-month charge is $160.00, which is 0.5 percent of the $32,000 balance, and later charges are smaller because the same 0.5 percent is applied to a balance that the earlier principal payments have reduced
lessons.distractor: The first-month charge is $160.00 and the later charges are smaller because the lender reduces the contractual rate as the loan ages
lessons.correction: The arithmetic is right and the reason is wrong. The rate does not change on a fixed-rate loan. Interest each period is the periodic rate multiplied by the balance outstanding, so the only quantity that moves is the balance. In month 18 the balance is small enough that 0.5 percent of it is $88.02, and by month 36 it is $4.84. Holding the rate fixed and shrinking the base is the entire mechanism, and confusing the base with the rate leads people to expect savings from refinancing that a late-term schedule cannot deliver.

depth.definitions: Amortization is the schedule by which a debt is repaid with interest in level payments; the same word also describes spreading a cost over time in accounting, which is a different use. Principal is the amount borrowed and still outstanding. Interest is the lender's charge, computed each period as the periodic rate multiplied by the balance outstanding in that period. The periodic rate is the annual rate divided by the number of periods per year, so 6 percent a year with monthly payments gives 0.5 percent a month. The term or maturity is the number of periods the schedule is built to. An amortization schedule lists the payment, interest, principal and remaining balance for every period. Prepayment is any payment above the scheduled amount. A balloon loan defers a large part of the principal to the end, so it is not fully amortizing. Negative amortization occurs when the scheduled payment is below the interest due, so the balance grows. Escrow is a separate account that collects money for taxes and insurance; it is part of the total monthly payment but not part of the loan's amortization.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is an identity, not a convention. In each period interest equals the periodic rate times the opening balance, and the closing balance equals the opening balance minus whatever the payment has left after interest. A level payment must therefore cover a large interest charge early and a small one late, which forces the principal portion to rise mechanically. That is why the interest profile of a level-payment loan is front-loaded and why the final payments are almost pure principal. Three limits matter. First, the schedule is an output of the contract's own conventions: the periodic rate may be the annual rate divided by twelve or an actual-over-365 day count, which is small per month and material over decades. Second, fees and insurance are not amortization. The Bureau's page on principal and interest against total monthly payment sets out that the total is principal plus interest plus mortgage insurance where applicable plus escrow for property taxes and insurance, that the principal and interest part generally stays level while the escrow part can change as taxes change, and that many buyers look only at principal and interest and are surprised by the total. A loan can be nearly paid off and still carry a monthly payment. Third, the schedule assumes every payment is made on time and nothing is added to the debt; a missed payment, a rate reset, a deferral or a new advance all require the schedule to be rebuilt.
depth.secondExample: Use one schedule to price three decisions instead of one. Decision one, term. The same $32,000 at 6 percent costs $3,046.07 of interest over 36 months and $5,118.98 over 60 months, so the 60-month payment is $354.85 lower and the extra interest is $2,072.91; the schedule states the exchange rate between liquidity and cost in dollars. Decision two, rate. At 8 percent over 36 months the payment is $1,002.76 and total interest is $4,099.49, so two percentage points cost $29.26 a month and $1,053.42 over the term on an unchanged balance. Decision three, prepayment. The extra $100 a month clears the loan three months early and saves $307.13, which is modest in proportion precisely because the interest still ahead after month 33 is thin. Now contrast a household comparing the same two terms using interest per year rather than total interest: $1,015.36 a year on the 36-month schedule against $1,023.80 a year on the 60-month schedule, which makes the two look almost identical. They are not. The 60-month borrower holds the debt two extra years and pays $2,072.91 more, so annualising a front-loaded cost over a longer life hides the information the schedule carries.
depth.mistake: The dominant error is treating the rate as a multiplier on the principal over the term. Multiplying 6 percent by three years by $32,000 gives $5,760 of expected interest, which is 89 percent higher than the actual $3,046.07, because that method charges interest on money already repaid. A second error is reading the payment as a measure of cost: the 60-month loan has the smaller payment and the larger cost, so ranking offers by payment size ranks them backwards on price. A third is assuming the split is constant, which leads people to expect large savings from refinancing late in a term and to attack the obligation with the gentlest payment first. A diagnostic that catches all three: write the opening balance for the period in question, multiply by the periodic rate, and ask whether the interest about to be paid is large or small relative to the payment. If it is small, prepaying that obligation saves little and money aimed there may be better aimed elsewhere. Confirm the periodic rate, the payment timing and any fees from the contract before relying on any of the arithmetic above.
depth.application: Build one schedule by hand or in a spreadsheet for a real or realistic level-payment obligation. Record the amount, the annual rate, the rate convention, the number of periods, the payment timing and every excluded fee. Produce four lines: first period, middle period, last period, and total interest over the term. Then answer three questions in writing. Which single period carries the largest interest charge, and why? What is the total interest if the term were one year longer, and what does that extra year buy? How much would an extra payment of one percent of the principal each period save, and does that saving change how you rank this obligation against any other you hold? Self-review rubric: the work is complete when the periodic rate is written as an explicit number, interest and principal are shown separately for each of the four periods, total interest reconciles to payments minus principal, and every exclusion such as fees, insurance, escrow or taxes is listed. It fails if any interest figure was estimated rather than computed, if the rate convention is unstated, or if the conclusion ranks two obligations by payment size alone. This is arithmetic on stated assumptions and not a recommendation about which obligation to hold.
depth.summary: A level payment is fixed while its contents are not. Interest each period is the periodic rate applied to the opening balance, so as the balance falls the interest falls and the principal portion rises. Three results follow: total interest is far below rate times principal times time, interest is concentrated in the early periods, and a smaller payment can buy a far larger cost. Read the schedule rather than the payment, and state the assumptions the schedule depends on.

lessons.title: One borrowed dollar, four different numbers: stated rate, effective rate, APR, and factor rate
lessons.explanation: Borrowed money is priced with several numbers that are not interchangeable, and the first analytical skill is knowing which question each one answers. A stated or nominal annual rate tells you the rate the contract names per year but says nothing about how often it compounds. An effective annual rate includes compounding inside the year, which is why OpenStax warns that because compounding occurs more than once a year the true annual rate is higher than it appears, and that the stated and effective rates are equal only when compounding is annual. An annual percentage rate goes further: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains that the APR is the interest rate plus any additional fees charged by the lender, including origination charges and other fees charged when the loan is made, and it warns that lenders must disclose the APR under the federal Truth in Lending Act so that you can compare loans, but only if you compare APRs to APRs and not APRs to interest rates. Regulation Z, the federal rule set that implements that framework, opens its definition by describing the APR as a measure of the cost of credit, expressed as a yearly rate, that relates the amount and timing of value received by the consumer to the amount and timing of payments made. That clause about timing is the whole point. A factor rate does none of this. The Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy explains that with a merchant cash advance a business receives a sum and pays it back based on a factor rate, which is a multiple of the amount borrowed, and that although a factor rate might seem identical to an interest rate the two are distinct, because the factor rate is applied to the whole amount borrowed at the beginning of the advance and does not reflect the decreasing amount owed as the borrower pays it back.
lessons.example: Hold the same transaction still and change only the number you use. Compounding first. An assumed 6 percent nominal rate compounded monthly is 6.1678 percent effective, because each month applies one twelfth of 6 percent to a growing balance; compounded semiannually it is 6.09 percent. A card stating 1.5 percent per month is 19.56 percent effective, which is what OpenStax gets from the same calculation in its stated-versus-effective section, and its point is that the intuitive answer of 1.5 percent times 12, or 18 percent, is not the rate the borrower pays. Now the factor rate. An assumed $10,000 advance at a factor of 1.30 requires $13,000 in total, a cost of $3,000. If the repayment is spread evenly over 6 months at $2,166.67 a month, the internal rate of return is 8.0535 percent a month, which is 96.64 percent a year on a nominal basis. Spread the same $13,000 over 12 monthly payments of $1,083.33 and the monthly rate falls to 4.2869 percent, or 51.44 percent a year. Spread it over 9 months and it is 5.5954 percent a month, or 67.15 percent a year. Divide the same total into 132 daily payments of $98.48 and the per-payment rate is 0.4140 percent, which annualises to 109.29 percent. One factor rate, four annualised answers between 51 and 109 percent, because the number of payments and their timing changed. Compare that with the SBA brief's own illustration that $10,000 over 12 months at a 10 percent APR pays about $550 of interest rather than the $1,000 that 10 percent of the original suggests; the installment schedule compounds down the declining balance, and recomputing it gives $879.16 a month and $549.91 of interest. Timing is not a detail. It is most of the number.
lessons.question: Two offers both quote a factor rate of 1.30 on $10,000. Offer A is repaid in 6 equal monthly payments and Offer B in 12 equal monthly payments. A reviewer writes that the two offers cost the same because the factor rate is identical. What is wrong with that reasoning?
lessons.answer: The total cost is the same, $3,000 in each case, but the annualised cost is not: the 6-month schedule implies about 96.64 percent a year and the 12-month schedule about 51.44 percent, because the money is held for different lengths of time
lessons.distractor: The two offers do not cost the same, because the 12-month schedule accumulates twice as much interest and therefore costs about $6,000
lessons.correction: A factor rate applies a fixed multiple to the amount advanced, so the dollar cost is $3,000 under both schedules; what changes is how long the borrower keeps the money. Six equal payments of $2,166.67 imply a monthly internal rate of 8.0535 percent, which annualises to 96.64 percent, while twelve payments of $1,083.33 imply 4.2869 percent a month, or 51.44 percent. The distractor treats the factor rate as if it accrued like an interest rate on the whole balance for the whole term, which is the error the factor rate's structure invites. Neither figure is an APR in the regulatory sense; both are annualised measures computed from stated assumptions.

depth.definitions: A stated or nominal rate is the annual rate named in the contract. An effective annual rate is what a nominal rate becomes when compounding inside the year is included. A simple or nominal annualisation multiplies a per-period rate by the number of periods in a year without compounding. An APR is defined in the United States by Regulation Z as a measure of the cost of credit, expressed as a yearly rate, that relates the amount and timing of value received to the amount and timing of payments made, and it is computed by the actuarial method or the United States Rule method. A finance charge is the cost of credit expressed in dollars. An origination fee is a charge for making the loan. A factor rate is a multiple applied to the amount advanced, so 1.30 means $1.30 owed for every $1.00 advanced. Amortising payments are equal installments; a lump-sum repayment is a single payment at the end. The internal rate of return is the discount rate that makes the present value of the payments equal the amount received. Accuracy of a disclosed APR is judged against tolerances: Regulation Z treats an APR as accurate if it is not more than one eighth of one percentage point above or below the computed rate, and one quarter of a point in an irregular transaction with multiple advances, irregular payment periods or irregular payment amounts.
depth.mechanism: Each number answers a different question, and the questions themselves differ in what they include. The stated rate answers what the contract names. The effective rate answers what a year of compounding does to that name. The APR answers what the whole transaction costs per year once fees are inside and the timing of payments is respected, which is why the regulatory definition is written as a relationship between the amount and timing of value received and the amount and timing of payments rather than as a rate applied to a principal. A factor rate answers none of those: it fixes a total to be repaid and leaves timing to the collection mechanism, which for a merchant cash advance is often a share of daily or weekly sales, so the calendar itself depends on the borrower's revenue. That is why one factor rate can correspond to annualised rates from about 51 percent to about 109 percent depending on the schedule. Three limits belong here. First, the one eighth of a point tolerance in Regulation Z is a rule about whether a disclosure is accurate, not a limit on what may be charged, and it is written for consumer credit; whether a commercial financing contract must disclose an APR at all depends on the law that applies to the product, the lender and the jurisdiction, and some jurisdictions have enacted commercial disclosure requirements while others have not. Second, the APR depends on which fees are included and on the assumed term, so two lenders can compute different APRs for the same product and both be internally consistent. Third, an annualised rate is not a forecast: it describes the cost of the credit as contracted, not what the borrower's revenue will do.
depth.secondExample: Watch the lower stated rate buy the more expensive loan. Offer one: $30,000 at an assumed 7 percent nominal, 24 monthly payments, with $1,200 of fees deducted at the start, so the borrower receives $28,800. The payment is $1,343.18, total payments are $32,236.26, and the all-in cost measured against the money actually received is $3,436.26. Discounting the payment stream against $28,800 gives a monthly rate of 0.9221 percent, which annualises to 11.07 percent. Offer two: the same $30,000 for the same 24 months at an assumed 8.5 percent, with only $150 of fees, so the borrower receives $29,850. The payment is $1,363.67 and total payments are $32,728.09, slightly more in total interest than offer one. Yet the all-in cost against money received is $2,878.09, and discounting against $29,850 gives 0.7499 percent a month, or 9.00 percent a year. The offer with the higher stated rate is the cheaper transaction by both measures once fees and net proceeds are inside the comparison, and no amount of staring at 7 percent against 8.5 percent reveals that. Now reverse one assumption: if the fees on offer one were 1.5 percent of the amount plus a fixed $250, the fee total would be $700, the all-in cost would fall to $2,936.26, and the two offers would be close enough that the term and the prepayment terms would decide between them.
depth.mistake: The classic error is annualising a factor rate by multiplying it, or by doubling it for a six-month term. A 1.30 factor over six months becomes 30 percent for the half year and therefore 60 percent a year under that method, which understates the amortising schedule's roughly 96.64 percent and understates the daily-repayment variant still further. A second error is comparing a stated rate with an APR, which the Bureau warns against in as many words: comparing APRs to APRs is valid, comparing an APR to an interest rate is not. A third is assuming an APR exists where it does not, since a commercial contract may lawfully price by factor rate and disclose no APR at all. A diagnostic that separates these cases: for each number on the page, write down what is in the numerator, what is in the denominator, and what timing assumption is buried inside it. If the denominator is the amount approved rather than the amount received, the number is flattering. If no timing appears in the definition, the number cannot be compared with anything that annualises. If you cannot name the governing rule that requires the number to be disclosed, treat it as marketing rather than measurement.
depth.application: Take one real or realistic offer and produce a four-line comparison sheet. Line one: the stated rate and the compounding convention. Line two: the effective annual rate you compute from line one. Line three: the annualised rate you compute by discounting the actual payment schedule against the money actually received, stating the fee schedule you deducted. Line four: the factor rate or total repayment figure if the product uses one, with the number of payments and their frequency. Then write two sentences: which line is missing from the offer document, and what assumption you had to supply to compute it. Self-review rubric: the sheet is complete when every computed rate states its compounding convention, when the amount received is reconciled to the amount approved minus named fees, and when no rate is compared with a rate computed on a different convention. It fails if a factor rate has been converted by multiplying rather than by discounting the payment schedule, if an APR is presented as a legal guarantee, or if a jurisdiction-specific disclosure requirement is asserted without naming the rule. Note in writing that this exercise measures the cost of credit as contracted and says nothing about whether the borrowing is affordable.
depth.summary: Four numbers describe four different things. The stated rate names a rate, the effective rate adds compounding, the APR relates the timing of value received to the timing of payments with fees included, and a factor rate fixes a total to be repaid while leaving timing to the repayment mechanism. Because timing drives the annualised answer, one factor rate can imply very different annual rates: the same 1.30 on $10,000 implies about 96.64 percent over a six-month equal-payment schedule and about 51.44 percent over twelve months. Compare like with like, state which fees are inside, and treat every annualised figure as arithmetic under stated assumptions rather than as a fact about the market.

readings.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, What is the difference between a loan interest rate and the APR?
readings.note: Read the whole page, which is short and is the anchor for this lesson's central distinction. readings.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, 12 CFR 1026.22 Determination of annual percentage rate
readings.note: Read paragraph (a) in full and paragraph (b) at least in outline. Paragraph (a)(1) is the operative definition: the annual percentage rate is a measure of the cost of credit, expressed as a yearly rate, that relates the amount and timing of value received by the consumer to the amount and timing of payments made, determined by the actuarial method or the United States Rule method, with the equations in appendix J to the part. lessons.title: Gross is not what you receive: fees, holdbacks, and net proceeds
lessons.explanation: The amount approved is a headline; the amount available is a measurement. Fees are deducted at the start of a financing, so the borrower's usable money is the approved amount minus those fees, which is the net proceeds. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's guide to comparing mortgage offers sets out where to find each piece on a Loan Estimate: the loan amount, the interest rate, the monthly principal and interest payment, mortgage insurance where applicable, the total monthly payment including escrow for property taxes and homeowners insurance, the upfront loan costs listed in Section D with particular attention to origination charges in Section A, lender credits in Section J, and the cash to close on page 2, which is what is actually needed at closing. The Bureau also gives a method rather than a single ratio: because borrowers on average keep a mortgage about five years, find the line for five years in the Comparisons section on page 3, take the first number, which is the total dollars paid including principal, subtract the second number, which is the principal paid off, and the difference is the interest and fees paid over five years. That subtraction is the same idea as net proceeds read in the other direction: what matters is the money that actually changed hands, not the amounts written at the top of the form. Regulation Z's content rule for the Loan Estimate is the underlying disclosure requirement, and it is worth reading for how many separate items must be stated before anyone can compare two offers honestly.
lessons.example: Price one facility twice, once against gross and once against what the borrower received. An assumed $25,000 twelve-month facility carries a 3 percent origination charge of $750 and a $500 documentation fee, so total fees are $1,250 and net proceeds are $23,750. At an assumed 9 percent nominal rate on the $25,000, the monthly payment is $2,186.29, total payments are $26,235.44, and total interest is $1,235.44. Read against the gross amount, that looks like a 9 percent loan with about 4.9 percent of interest over the year. Read against net proceeds, the borrower paid $26,235.44 for $23,750 of usable money, so the all-in cost is $2,485.44, which is 10.47 percent of what was received. Discounting the same twelve payments of $2,186.29 against $23,750 gives a monthly rate of 1.5654 percent, or 18.79 percent annualised, more than double the stated 9 percent. Scale the same structure up: a $100,000 facility with a 2 percent arrangement fee and a 1 percent advisory fee deducts $3,000 and delivers $97,000. Now the fee-added trap. If the borrower instead takes a $10,000 advance at a factor of 1.30 but the fees of $1,000 are added to the amount advanced, the factor applies to a face amount of $11,000, giving $14,300 to repay on $10,000 received: a cost of $4,300, which on six equal monthly payments of $2,383.33 implies a monthly rate of 11.29 percent, or 135.44 percent annualised. Every figure assumes the stated fee schedule, end-of-month payments, no prepayment, no rate reset, no late charges and no additional advances.
lessons.question: A lender advertises $25,000 at 9 percent for twelve months and deducts $1,250 of origination and documentation fees at the start. A borrower receives $23,750 and pays $2,186.29 a month. Which statement describes the cost correctly?
lessons.answer: Measuring the same payments against the $23,750 actually received gives an annualised cost of about 18.79 percent, and the all-in cost of $2,485.44 is 10.47 percent of the money received
lessons.distractor: The cost is 9 percent plus the fees expressed as a rate, so 9 percent plus 5 percent of the amount for a total of 14 percent for the year
lessons.correction: Adding a fee percentage to the stated rate treats the fee as if it were interest spread evenly over the year, which is not how it behaves. The fee is paid once at the start and the money that was withheld is never available for use, so the same payment stream buys less. Discounting the twelve payments of $2,186.29 against $23,750 gives 1.5654 percent a month, or 18.79 percent annualised, well above the 14 percent the distractor arrives at. The direction of the distractor is right, since fees raise the true cost above the stated rate, but the method understates the result because it ignores that the withheld money would have been held for the whole term.

depth.definitions: Net proceeds are the funds actually made available to a borrower after deductions, often described as cash to close in mortgage disclosure. Gross proceeds or the loan amount are the headline figures. An origination charge is a lender fee for making the loan. Discount points are an upfront payment that buys a lower rate. Lender credits are rebates that offset closing costs at the price of a higher rate. A documentation or underwriting fee is a fixed administrative charge. Third-party costs, such as appraisal, title or filing fees, are paid to others but still reduce proceeds. A holdback or reserve is money withheld until a condition is met or remaining as required collateral; it is not a fee if it can be released. A compensating balance is a deposit the lender requires the borrower to keep, which raises the effective cost of the money actually usable. An arrangement or advisory fee is a charge for structuring, common in commercial facilities. The break-even period is how long the savings from paying a fee must accrue before the fee is recovered.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is that a fee is paid once while a rate is charged per period, so a fee's weight depends on how long the money is held. Spread a $1,250 fee over a twelve-month facility and it adds roughly 5 percent of the face amount to the year's cost; spread the same fee over five years and its annual claim roughly a fifth of that, which is why the Bureau's five-year cost of borrowing comparison is a fairer basis for a product most borrowers keep about five years. Two further mechanisms matter. First, direction of travel: prepaying a loan does not refund the fee, so a short holding period raises the effective cost sharply, and a facility that also forbids prepayment converts that arithmetic into a contractual fact. Second, the base: a rate covers the amount outstanding, while a fee is usually charged on the amount approved, so fees applied to a grossed-up principal that includes the fees themselves compound the problem, as the factor example shows. Limits: fees can buy something real, and a discount point that reduces the rate is not waste; the comparison must therefore be between two offers priced over the same horizon for the same net proceeds. Jurisdiction and product type decide whether any of this must be disclosed, since consumer credit and commercial credit are governed differently.
depth.secondExample: Test whether a fee buys its keep. An assumed $300,000 thirty-year loan at 6.5 percent has a monthly principal and interest payment of $1,896.20; at 6.0 percent the payment is $1,798.65. The difference is $97.55 a month, so paying $1,200 in points to buy the lower rate is recovered after 1,200 divided by 97.55, which is 12.3 months, and over the full thirty years the lower rate saves $35,118.90 of interest. On that arithmetic the points pay for themselves within about a year, provided the borrower keeps the loan that long and the points are genuinely the only difference between the two offers. Now run the same test on a shorter horizon, which is the case the Bureau warns about: if the borrower refinances or sells after three years, the recovery still happens, because 12.3 months is inside three years, but the thirty-year saving of $35,118.90 is never collected. Reverse the fee scale and the answer flips: if the same lower rate cost $2,600 in points, recovery would take 26.7 months, and a two-year holding period would leave the borrower worse off by about $259 plus the cost of the refinancing. The lesson is not that points are good or bad but that the break-even period, computed from the payment difference, has to be compared with a stated holding period.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is comparing offers by their stated rates when the fee schedules differ, which the example above shows can produce the wrong ranking entirely. The second is treating a holdback as a fee: a reserve that is released on a condition reduces cash available now but not the cost of the money, and booking it as a cost double-counts it. The third is grossing up the principal to cover fees and then pricing the larger amount, so that the borrower pays interest and fees on the withheld money; the $10,000 advance at a factor applied to $11,000 is the cleanest illustration, because the effective annualised cost rises to about 135 percent on the money actually received. A diagnostic that catches all three: write two columns, one headed approved and one headed received, and put every dollar that moves in exactly one of them, then compute the total dollars paid from the received column only. If a figure appears in both columns or in neither, the sheet is wrong. Confirm from the document which charges are lender charges, which are third-party costs and which are refundable before treating any of them as a cost.
depth.application: Build a proceeds sheet for one real or realistic offer. Three rows at the top: the amount approved, each deduction with the name used in the offer document, and the resulting net proceeds, reconciled so the first row minus the second equals the third. Then three rows below: the full payment schedule, the total dollars to be paid, and the all-in cost defined as total dollars paid minus net proceeds. Then a final row stating the all-in cost as a percentage of net proceeds and the annualised rate obtained by discounting the payment schedule against net proceeds. Finish with two sentences: which single deduction costs the most per dollar received, and which fee on the document you could not classify as refundable or non-refundable. Self-review rubric: complete when net proceeds are reconciled to the approved amount, when the annualised figure is computed from the received amount rather than the approved amount, and when every deduction is labelled with the name the document uses. It fails if a stated rate alone is offered as the cost, if a holdback is counted as a fee, or if the percentage of net proceeds and the annualised rate are presented as if they were the same measure. This measures the cost of credit as contracted; it does not assess affordability.
depth.summary: A financing has a headline and a delivery. Fees withheld at the start mean the usable money is smaller than the approved amount, and the cost that matters is total dollars paid divided by dollars received, annualised on the actual payment schedule. The same payments that look like a 9 percent loan against $25,000 imply about 18.79 percent against the $23,750 received. Compare offers over the same horizon for the same net proceeds, check whether each fee is refundable, and watch for fees added to a principal that is then priced again.

lessons.title: Reconstructing cash from records: profit is a timing opinion, cash is a fact
lessons.explanation: Two true numbers can disagree. Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not money has moved; under the cash method, income and expenses are counted when money is received and paid. OpenStax's financial accounting walkthrough of the statement of cash flows makes the consequence explicit: accrual accounting records transactions when they occur and not necessarily when cash moves, and that creates a timing difference. The IRS Publication 538 heading structure for accounting periods and methods sets out the same architecture from the tax side, listing the cash method with constructive receipt for income and payments in advance for expenses, the accrual method with economic performance for expenses, and the hybrid method. The reconciliation between the two views is not a matter of opinion, because the differences are exactly the balances that sit between earning and paying: receivables, payables, inventory, prepayments and non-cash charges such as depreciation. The statement of cash flows separates movements into operating, investing and financing activities, and OpenStax notes that assessing how much a business relies on each of those three sources is how a reader judges its ability to generate profit and stay in business. For a household or a small firm, the same discipline applies with fewer categories. Start from the bank and payment records, classify every movement, and then explain the gap between the accounting result and the cash result line by line. A gap that cannot be explained by a named balance is either an error or a missing record, and both need to be found before the numbers are used to make a decision.
lessons.example: Reconstruct one month from records alone. Invoices issued for work completed total $42,000, of which $36,500 was collected, so receivables rose by $5,500. Expenses recognised in the same month total $31,000, and $900 of that is depreciation on equipment, which is a non-cash charge. Payables rose by $900, meaning $900 of recognised expenses had not yet been paid. Inventory purchased for cash during the month was $3,400, which is an asset change and not an expense. Accounting profit is $42,000 minus $31,000, which is $11,000. Cash from operations can be built the direct way: collections of $36,500 minus cash expenses of $29,200 minus inventory purchases of $3,400, which is $3,900. It can also be built the indirect way: start from $11,000, subtract the $5,500 increase in receivables, add back the $900 of depreciation, add the $900 increase in payables, and subtract the $3,400 inventory purchase, which also gives $3,900. The bridge is exact: 5,500 minus 900 minus 900 plus 3,400 equals 7,100, which is the gap between $11,000 of profit and $3,900 of cash. Now use the number. If cash on hand is $21,000 and the monthly cash outflow exceeds cash receipts by $1,150 on average, the runway is 21,000 divided by 1,150, or 18.3 months, before any new borrowing or new revenue. And watch the timing: a quarterly tax or insurance deposit of $4,350 landing in one month turns that month's outflow into $5,500 and shortens the runway by roughly 3.8 months if sustained. Assumptions: one month, no borrowing, no owner draws, no capital expenditure, no tax accruals beyond those named, and no change in payment terms during the period.
lessons.question: A firm reports $11,000 of profit for a month and $3,900 of cash from operations. Which explanation accounts for the entire $7,100 difference?
lessons.answer: Receivables rose $5,500 and inventory purchased for cash was $3,400, while depreciation of $900 and a $900 rise in payables both add back, so 5,500 minus 900 minus 900 plus 3,400 equals 7,100
lessons.distractor: The $7,100 gap is unexplained rounding and timing noise that should be written off as immaterial at this scale
lessons.correction: The gap is fully explained by four named balances, each of which is visible in the records. Receivables rose because $5,500 of invoiced work had not been collected, which is cash the business has earned but not received. Inventory purchased for cash is an outflow that never appears as an expense in the month it is bought. Depreciation reduced profit without using any cash, so it is added back. Payables rose by $900 because a recognised expense had not been paid. Adding the four effects gives exactly $7,100, and any residual left after naming them has to be a missing record or an error rather than an immaterial difference.

depth.definitions: Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred. The cash method records income when received and expenses when paid. Constructive receipt is the tax concept that income is treated as received when it is credited to the taxpayer or made available without restriction, even if the cheque is not banked. Economic performance is the accrual-side condition for when an expense is treated as incurred. Receivables are amounts owed to the business by customers; payables are amounts it owes to suppliers. A prepayment is money paid before the cost is incurred, such as an annual insurance premium. Inventory is goods held for sale, an asset until sold. Depreciation is the allocation of a capital asset's cost across periods; it is a non-cash charge. Free cash flow is operating cash flow reduced by capital expenditure, which is why OpenStax's treatment of a misclassified transaction matters: putting a non-cash investing and financing transaction into the cash statement distorts it. Operating, investing and financing activities are the three categories of the statement of cash flows. Runway is the number of months cash on hand covers the current net outflow.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is that profit and cash are computed from different events. Profit asks what was earned and incurred in a period; cash asks what moved. Every difference between them must sit in one of a small number of places: a receivable, a payable, an inventory balance, a prepayment, an accrued liability, or a non-cash charge. That is why the bridge can be built from either direction and must agree. OpenStax's discussion of the three activity categories adds the second mechanism: the same total cash movement can come from operations, from selling assets or from borrowing, and a business financed mainly by the third of those is in a different position from one that generates cash from the first, even if both report identical net cash. Two limits belong here. First, the classification depends on conventions and on judgement: a transaction can be reported in more than one defensible way, which is why the source's own example of a non-cash purchase misclassified into both the investing and financing sections matters for any reader computing free cash flow from the statement. Second, the reconstruction is only as good as the records: payments made in cash, informal loans between the owner and the business, or invoices never issued cannot be recovered from bank statements, so the result should carry an explicit statement of what is missing rather than an adjustment for it.
depth.secondExample: Run the same reconstruction for a business with the opposite pattern, one that collects before it delivers and pays late. Deposits received in advance total $28,000 in a month in which only $19,000 of work was completed and invoiced, so deferred revenue rises by $9,000. Bills from suppliers for $22,000 arrive and are recognised, but only $15,000 is paid, so payables rise by $7,000. There is no depreciation and no inventory. Profit for the month is $19,000 minus $22,000, a loss of $3,000. Cash from operations is $28,000 minus $15,000, an inflow of $13,000. The bridge is inverted: 9,000 plus 7,000 equals 16,000, which is exactly the gap between a $3,000 loss and $13,000 of cash. The business has cash and no profit, and both statements are right. The analytical question differs from the first example. Where the first business had to convert profit into cash, this one has to convert cash into delivery, and its risk is that the work owed is larger than the cash held: $9,000 of deposits is an obligation to perform, and if delivery costs more than assumed the cash already looks spent. Run the runway calculation the same way but add a second line for unearned obligations, because treating deposits as ordinary available cash overstates the cushion.
depth.mistake: The most common error is reading the bank balance as profit: a healthy balance can sit on top of unpaid payables and unearned deposits, and an empty balance can sit on top of large receivables. The second is annualising a partial period, which fails badly wherever an expense or a receipt is seasonal; multiplying three months of a seasonal cost by four creates an expense that does not exist. The third is treating a non-cash charge as if it were cash, in either direction: depreciation does not consume cash, but the asset it represents did, and a loan repayment reduces cash without reducing profit, so neither can be ignored. A diagnostic that catches all three: take the difference between profit and operating cash, and keep naming balances until the two reconcile exactly. If the residual will not close, list the records you do not have. A sheet that reconciles only after an entry labelled miscellaneous has not reconciled, because the entire purpose of the exercise is to attribute every dollar to a named event.
depth.application: Take the most recent three months of bank and payment records and rebuild operating cash for each month, direct method, using only what the records support: receipts, payments to suppliers, payroll, rent, tax deposits, fees. Then produce the indirect bridge for the same three months, naming each balance that explains the gap between the accounting result and the cash result. With what is left over, compute the average monthly net outflow and divide cash on hand by it to get a runway in months, and separately list every known irregular payment in the next twelve months with the month it lands in. Self-review rubric: complete when each month reconciles to the cent in both directions, when every bridging item is named and traced to a specific record, when the runway states its assumption about future net outflow, and when a written list names the movements the records cannot capture, such as cash payments or owner loans. It fails if any residual is absorbed without a named cause, if a partial period is annualised without a seasonal adjustment note, or if the runway is presented as a forecast rather than as arithmetic on the current outflow.
depth.summary: Profit and cash answer different questions, and the difference between them is always explained by named balances. Receivables, payables, inventory, prepayments and non-cash charges form a bridge that must close exactly in both directions. The same set of records supports a runway calculation and a list of irregular payments, but only if every movement is attributed and the records that are missing are declared. Reconstructing the bridge is what turns a bank balance into information.

lessons.title: Ratios are measurements, not verdicts: liquidity, solvency and coverage
lessons.explanation: A ratio converts two numbers into one and makes comparison possible, which is its whole purpose and its whole limit. OpenStax's chapter on measures of financial health puts it plainly: financial ratios help internal and external stakeholders make informed decisions about actions such as investing, becoming a supplier, making a loan or altering internal operations, and they allow trends to be examined, benchmarks to be set and competitors to be compared; converting information to percentages or ratios eliminates some of the disparities between competitors' sizes and operating abilities. The same chapter then spends a section on limitations, and those limitations are the reason this lesson exists: past performance does not always predict future performance, economic conditions can distort the data being analysed, the way a company reports information may change over time in ways that are not immediately evident, and although publicly traded firms in the United States follow generally accepted accounting principles, many standards contain estimates and flexibility, so two firms can both follow the standards and present information differently. The four families are liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability. This lesson works on one consumer and one business measure in each of two families, because the arithmetic transfers: a debt-to-income ratio and a debt-to-assets ratio are the same shape of measurement applied to a household and to a firm, and a household's coverage of its obligations is the same question a lender asks of a business as times interest earned or debt service coverage.
lessons.example: Compute six measurements from one set of records, then stress one of them. Liquidity: current assets of $48,000 against current liabilities of $30,000 give a current ratio of 1.60, and after removing $26,000 of inventory from the numerator the quick ratio is $22,000 against $30,000, or 0.73. Solvency: total liabilities of $250,000 against total assets of $400,000 give a debt-to-assets ratio of 62.5 percent, and the same liabilities against equity of $150,000 give a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.67, which reports the same information in a different shape. Coverage: earnings before interest and tax of $84,000 against interest of $21,000 give times interest earned of 4.0 times, and net operating income of $96,000 against debt service of $72,000 gives a debt service coverage ratio of 1.33. Profitability: revenue of $420,000 with $260,000 of cost of goods sold gives a gross margin of 38.1 percent, and net income of $26,000 gives a net margin of 6.2 percent. Consumer side: monthly obligations of $1,850 against gross monthly income of $5,400 give a debt-to-income ratio of 34.26 percent. Now stress the solvency measure. If $250,000 of the debt is floating and the rate rises two percentage points, interest rises by $5,000 a year, and times interest earned falls from 4.0 to $84,000 divided by $26,000, or 3.23. The same business still shows a comfortable gross margin and a moderate debt-to-income ratio; one measure moved by 19 percent and the others did not move at all. Assumptions: one reporting date, no off-balance-sheet obligations, no unusual items removed, interest computed on the average balance, and the same accounting policies across all figures.
lessons.question: A lender says a firm is safe because its debt-to-assets ratio of 62.5 percent is below its stated limit of 65 percent, while another measure of the same firm gives times interest earned of 3.23 after a rate rise. How should the two measurements be read together?
lessons.answer: They measure different things: the first compares total debt with total assets at a point in time, while the second tests whether earnings can cover interest as it comes due, so a firm can pass a leverage test and still have thin coverage
lessons.distractor: The leverage ratio is the more reliable of the two, so the coverage figure can be set aside as a secondary indicator
lessons.correction: Both are measurements and neither is a verdict. A leverage ratio describes the composition of the balance sheet at a reporting date; a coverage ratio describes whether the earnings of a period are sufficient to pay the interest of that period. A firm can sit comfortably inside a leverage covenant and still fail to cover interest if earnings fall or if the rate on floating debt rises, which is exactly what the stress case shows when times interest earned drops from 4.0 to 3.23. Ignoring coverage because leverage looks acceptable removes the measure that responds first to a change in earnings or rates. Where the two disagree, the productive question is which assumption each one depends on.

depth.definitions: A liquidity ratio compares assets that will turn into cash soon with obligations due soon; the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, and the quick ratio removes inventory and other less liquid items. A solvency ratio compares total obligations with the resource base: debt-to-assets divides total liabilities by total assets, and debt-to-equity divides total liabilities by equity. Times interest earned divides earnings before interest and taxes by interest expense and reports how many times the period's earnings cover the interest. Debt service coverage divides net operating income by total debt service, where debt service is scheduled principal plus interest. A profitability ratio compares a profit measure with a revenue or asset base: gross margin uses revenue minus cost of goods sold over revenue, and net margin uses net income over revenue. Debt-to-income divides monthly debt payments by gross monthly income. A benchmark is a comparison value from a peer group, an industry series or the firm's own history. A covenant is a contractual condition, often expressed as a ratio limit. Coverage and leverage are therefore not competing scores but different questions.
depth.mechanism: A ratio removes scale so that comparison is possible, and that removal is what limits it. Dividing by assets strips out size but also strips out composition, so a firm with old, fully depreciated assets and one with new assets can report the same debt-to-assets ratio while facing very different refinancing needs. A ratio is also silent about timing: current liabilities include amounts due next week and amounts due in eleven months, and current assets include inventory that may take months to convert. Three further limits follow from the sources. OpenStax notes that reporting itself can change in ways not immediately evident, so a ratio compared across two years may be comparing two accounting policies rather than two performances. It notes that standards contain estimates and flexibility, so both figures in the ratio may be the product of judgement. And it notes that economic conditions distort reported data, so a ratio measured in one part of a cycle is not a forecast. The practical consequence is that a ratio is only interpretable with three things attached: the formula used, the period measured, and the comparison group. A ratio missing any of the three is an anecdote with a decimal point.
depth.secondExample: Show how the same business produces two different liquidity pictures from one set of facts, depending on the date. A seasonal retailer holds inventory for a holiday quarter. At the end of the season, after inventory has been sold down and cash has been collected, current assets are $186,000 against current liabilities of $116,000, a current ratio of 1.60, which matches the first example. Six months later, before the buying season, the same firm has rebuilt inventory on supplier credit and paid down little: current assets are $252,000, including $176,000 of inventory, and current liabilities are $296,000, so the current ratio is 0.85. Nothing has gone wrong; the business is simply at a different point in its annual cycle. The quick ratio tells the story more sharply: at the year-end date it is $58,000 against $116,000, or 0.50, and before the season it is $76,000 against $296,000, or 0.26. A lender comparing only the favourable date with a peer group would be comparing a season with a season. The remedy is not a better formula but a better comparison: measure the ratio at the same point in the cycle in each year, state the inventory policy, and average the ratio across a full cycle where the cycle is known.
depth.mistake: The common errors are treating a ratio as a grade, and importing someone else's number as a target. A listed company's debt-to-equity ratio is not a standard for a service business, because capital intensity, cash-flow stability and access to equity all differ. A second error is comparing ratios computed with different definitions, which is why the source's own emphasis on the possibility of differently presented information matters: if inventory is net of an allowance in one period and gross in another, the quick ratio changes for reasons that have nothing to do with liquidity. A third is relying on a single date, which the seasonal example shows can be made to say almost anything. A diagnostic that catches the three: for every ratio, write the formula, the period, the source document for each input, and the comparison group, then compute the same ratio for three consecutive periods and see whether the story is stable. If any input came from a different accounting policy or a different point in the cycle, note it before drawing a conclusion. A ratio that cannot survive its own definitions sheet is not evidence.
depth.application: Compute six ratios from your own or a realistic set of records: current, quick, debt-to-assets, times interest earned, gross margin and debt-to-income. For each one, write the formula in full with the named inputs, the period, the document each input came from, and the comparison group you intend to use. Then stress two of them: recompute times interest earned after a two percentage point rise in the rate on floating debt, and recompute the current ratio after removing inventory. Finally, write down the one ratio you cannot compute and the record that would be needed to compute it. Self-review rubric: complete when every ratio shows its formula and its period, when each input is traceable to a named record, when the stress cases show before and after values, and when the missing ratio is named rather than estimated. It fails if a ratio is presented without its comparison group, if the figures are mixed across two different reporting policies, or if a conclusion about creditworthiness is drawn from points in time rather than from a sequence. Ratios measure; they do not decide.
depth.summary: Ratios make comparison possible by removing scale, and that is exactly what they cannot do: they hide composition, timing and accounting policy, and they describe a date rather than a future. Computed with stated formulas and compared against the same point in the cycle and a stated peer group, a small set of them is genuinely informative. Leverage and coverage are different questions, and a firm can pass one while failing the other, which is why the stress case matters more than the snapshot.

readings.title: OpenStax, Principles of Finance, 6.1 Ratios: Condensing Information into Smaller Pieces
readings.note: Read the whole section, including the part most readers skip. Read the opening point that outcomes need to be compared with similar data in the industry, with close competitors, and with the company's own past experience. Read Importance of Ratios and Analysis for the four main types of ratios, liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability, and the statement that the industry in which the business operates can change the influence of any outcome on a stakeholder decision. Read Limitation of Financial Statement Analysis in full, because this lesson is built on it: past performance does not always predict future performance; economic influences such as inflation or a recession can skew the data being analysed; the way a company reports information may change over time, including changes in where and when transactions are recorded, and this may not be immediately evident to users; and while US publicly traded companies must follow generally accepted accounting principles, there are many estimates and flexibility in how some standards are applied, so firms can follow the standards and still present information differently. Verified HTTP 200 and read.

readings.title: OpenStax, Principles of Finance, 6.4 Solvency Ratios
readings.note: Read the whole section. It defines solvency as the ability to meet long-term obligations and stay in business, then works the debt-to-assets ratio, explaining that it shows how much of the assets were financed with debt and that it includes both long-term debt and current liabilities, and that a ratio above 1.0 means more debt than assets and therefore negative equity. Read its worked figures and its warning that comparing the ratio with industry averages provides better insight, then read the debt-to-equity ratio and the section's observation that the two ratios contain the same information in different shapes, so an analyst may prefer one because of the format of available industry data. Read the Think It Through case about a covenant requiring debt-to-equity not to exceed 0.50 and how issuing debt versus issuing stock changes the ratio, since it shows a ratio operating as a contractual trigger rather than a description. Then read the times interest earned ratio, its definition from earnings before interest and taxes, and the statement that lenders pay attention to it before extending long-term credit. Verified HTTP 200 and read.

readings.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, What is a debt-to-income ratio?
readings.note: Read the whole page, which is short. It defines the ratio as monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, where gross monthly income is the amount earned before taxes and other deductions; it states that different loan products and lenders have different limits; and it gives a worked example in which $1,500 of mortgage payment plus a $100 auto loan plus $400 of other debts gives $2,000 of monthly debt payments against $6,000 of gross income, a ratio of 33 percent. Read it as the household version of the same measurement family as debt-to-assets and debt service coverage, and note the detail in the denominator: because it is gross income, the ratio is not the same as obligations divided by take-home pay, which is higher. Verified HTTP 200 and read.

readings.title: U.S. Small Business Administration, Manage your finances
readings.note: Read the balance sheet section and the cost-benefit analysis paragraph. The page states that the balance sheet is the foundation of managing finances, operates as a snapshot of business financials, helps keep track of capital and supports a cash flow projection, and helps track assets, liabilities and equity; it adds the encouragement to get insights by separating and analysing segments, such as comparing online sales with face-to-face sales. The cost-benefit paragraph describes weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a business decision after categorising expenses. Read it for how the raw materials of ratios are assembled, and note the page's framing of a snapshot, which is the same point this lesson makes about ratios describing a date rather than a future.
